Sample text:
---
The first time my mother forgot how to make rice, she called me and pretended she was conducting a survey.

“How much water do you use for one cup?”

“One and a half cups. Why?”

“And do you wash it?”

“You taught me to wash it.”

“I know what I taught you. I’m asking what you do.”

I could hear the pencil. For some reason that was what frightened me: she was writing it down.

“Depends who’s coming over,” I said. “If it’s just me, sometimes I don’t bother.”

“You should bother just for you.”

She hung up before I could ask her anything.

That Christmas I bought her a rice cooker. She already owned a rice cooker, as I discovered when I opened the cupboard to put mine away. The old one was a wedding present, cream-colored, with a little orange lever. It had made approximately half of my body. I had forgotten it existed.

“Well,” my mother said, watching me kneel on the kitchen floor between the two machines. “Runs in the family.”

We laughed much harder than the joke deserved. Neither of us wanted to be the first to stop.

By spring she had notes everywhere. Some were practical: GLASSES, KEYS, TUESDAY BINS. Others seemed to be addressed to a difficult employee. PLEASE FINISH ONE JOB BEFORE BEGINNING ANOTHER. There was a note on the back door saying CAT, although we had not owned a cat for eleven years.

“What am I supposed to do about the cat?” I asked.

“Oh, nothing. That one’s old.”

I reached to peel it off.

“Leave it,” she said. “I like thinking for half a second I have a cat.”

I left it.

One Sunday in June I found her at the table with a stack of index cards, trying to write down the things nobody else in the family knew. Where her father’s watch had gone. Which cousin still owed her forty dollars. The name of the woman in the photograph everybody thought was Aunt Lorna, including, when she was alive, Aunt Lorna.

“Is there anything you want to know?” she asked.

There were enormous things I wanted to know. Had she been happy with my father? Had she wanted another life? Which of the many things I had said to hurt her had actually hurt? But she had uncapped her pen and was waiting, and what came out was, “What did you put in the eggs at the beach?”

When I was nine we had rented a cottage for a week. It rained every day. My father got a fishhook through the pad of his thumb without having caught, or even seen, a fish. But the scrambled eggs my mother made on the last morning were so good that for years afterward my brother and I asked for beach eggs. She could never make them again.

She set down the pen. “I used the pan after the doughnuts.”

“What doughnuts?”

“You were asleep. Your father and I used to buy those plain doughnuts and fry them in butter. If you children had known, we’d have had to buy six. We could afford two.”

“All these years you let us think it was some kind of spice.”

“I forgot about the doughnuts.”

“But you remember now?”

“Apparently.”

I got up and looked in her bread bin. There were no doughnuts. We drove to the supermarket.

At home she cut one in half around its equator and set both halves facedown in a buttered frying pan. When the cut sides were brown we ate them standing at the counter. Then she cracked four eggs into the pan. I started to reach for the milk.

“Absolutely not,” she said.

We ate the eggs with the little forks she usually saved for company. They were fine. Faintly sweet in places. Not what I remembered.

“Well?” she asked.

I considered lying. “I think maybe you had to be nine.”

“And damp,” she said.

Afterward I washed up while she sat at the table and made out a card. I assumed she was writing down the recipe. When I went to put it in the box, I saw what she had written.

*June 12. Ellen came over. We had the doughnuts first this time, together.*

I read it twice. Until then I had thought of the cards as a way of getting things out of the house before the roof came down. It hadn’t occurred to me that she was still moving things in.

There were three doughnuts left in the bag. I put two in the freezer and took one home. On Monday morning I fried it before work. I used too much butter, which turned out to be a fairly minor error in the scheme of things. I ate both halves off a saucer with my little finger through the hole where the cup was meant to sit.

Then I washed the saucer. I was running late. I washed it just for me.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: VARY

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION — A literary short story built around a mother’s memory loss, family rituals, and the small acts that keep affection present.

## Grounded reading
The voice is intimate, observant, and quietly funny, letting grief and tenderness surface through practical details rather than explanation. The narrator’s attention to the pencil, the old rice cooker, the cat note, and the doughnuts gives ordinary objects the weight of shared history. The story invites the reader to notice that care can run both ways: the mother is recording what she might lose, while the narrator discovers that their time together is still adding something to the record.

## What the model chose to foreground
The piece foregrounds memory, aging, and the uneven ways family members know one another. Food and household objects—rice, eggs, doughnuts, index cards, a saucer—become vessels for inherited habits and intimate history. Its moral emphasis is modest rather than grand: making an effort for oneself, and treating time together as something still being made.

## Evidence line
> I washed it just for me.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — the recurring domestic details and the understated turn from loss toward shared creation make this a distinctive, carefully shaped piece rather than a generic sentimental story.
